englishChanges.evidence: Dostoevsky letter to Mikhail,22 December1849, https://rvb.ru/dostoevski/01text/vol15/01text/381.htm; independent letter editions confirm sword-breaking ceremony.

danish.source: A few words about Dostoevsky himself may help the English reader to understand his work.
danish.translation: Et par ord om Dostojevskij selv kan hjælpe den engelske læser til at forstå hans værk.

danish.source: Dostoevsky was the son of a doctor. His parents were very hard-working and deeply religious people, but so poor that they lived with their five children in only two rooms. The father and mother spent their evenings in reading aloud to their children, generally from books of a serious character.
danish.translation: Dostojevskij var søn af en læge. Hans forældre var meget arbejdsomme og dybt religiøse mennesker, men så fattige, at de boede med deres fem børn i blot to værelser. Om aftenen læste faren og moren højt for børnene, som regel af bøger med alvorligt indhold.

danish.source: Though always sickly and delicate Dostoevsky came out third in the final examination of the Petersburg school of Engineering. There he had already begun his first work, “Poor Folk.”
danish.translation: Selv om Dostojevskij altid var sygelig og skrøbelig, blev han nummer tre ved afgangseksamen fra ingeniørskolen i Sankt Petersborg. Her var han allerede begyndt på sit første værk, »Fattige folk«.

danish.source: This story was published by the poet Nekrassov in his review and was received with acclamations. The shy, unknown youth found himself instantly something of a celebrity. A brilliant and successful career seemed to open before him, but those hopes were soon dashed. In 1849 he was arrested.
danish.translation: Fortællingen blev udgivet af digteren Nekrasov i hans tidsskrift og modtaget med begejstring. Den generte, ukendte unge mand blev med ét lidt af en berømthed. En strålende og succesrig løbebane syntes at åbne sig for ham, men håbet blev snart knust. I 1849 blev han arresteret.

danish.source: Though neither by temperament nor conviction a revolutionist, Dostoevsky was one of a little group of young men who met together to read Fourier and Proudhon. He was accused of “taking part in conversations against the censorship, of reading a letter from Byelinsky to Gogol, and of knowing of the intention to set up a printing press.” Under Nicholas I. (that “stern and just man,” as Maurice Baring calls him) this was enough, and he was condemned to death. After eight months’ imprisonment he was with twenty-one others taken out to the Semyonovsky Square to be shot. Writing to his brother Mihail, Dostoevsky says: “They snapped swords over our heads, and they made us put on the white shirts worn by persons condemned to death. Thereupon we were bound in threes to stakes, to suffer execution. Being the third in the row, I concluded I had only a few minutes of life before me. I thought of you and your dear ones and I contrived to kiss Plestcheiev and Dourov, who were next to me, and to bid them farewell. Suddenly the troops beat a tattoo, we were unbound, brought back upon the scaffold, and informed that his Majesty had spared us our lives.” The sentence was commuted to hard labour.
danish.translation: Selv om Dostojevskij hverken af temperament eller overbevisning var revolutionær, tilhørte han en lille kreds af unge mænd, som mødtes for at læse Fourier og Proudhon. Han blev anklaget for »at have deltaget i samtaler imod censuren, læst et brev fra Belinskij til Gogol og kendt til hensigten om at oprette et trykkeri«. Under Nikolaj I — denne »strenge og retfærdige mand«, som Maurice Baring kalder ham — var det nok, og han blev dømt til døden. Efter otte måneders fængsel blev han sammen med enogtyve andre ført ud på Semjonovskij-pladsen for at blive skudt. I et brev til sin bror Mikhail skriver Dostojevskij: »De knækkede sværd over vores hoveder og lod os tage de hvide skjorter på, som dødsdømte bærer. Så blev vi bundet tre og tre til pæle for at blive henrettet. Da jeg stod som den tredje i rækken, regnede jeg med kun at have få minutter tilbage at leve i. Jeg tænkte på dig og dine kære, og det lykkedes mig at kysse Plesjtjejev og Durov, som stod ved siden af mig, og sige farvel til dem. Pludselig slog soldaterne signal på tromme; vi blev løst fra rebene, ført tilbage til skafottet og fik at vide, at Hans Majestæt havde skånet vores liv.« Dommen blev ændret til strafarbejde.

danish.source: One of the prisoners, Grigoryev, went mad as soon as he was untied, and never regained his sanity.
danish.translation: En af fangerne, Grigorjev, mistede forstanden, så snart han blev løst fra rebene, og blev aldrig rask igen.

danish.source: The intense suffering of this experience left a lasting stamp on Dostoevsky’s mind. Though his religious temper led him in the end to accept every suffering with resignation and to regard it as a blessing in his own case, he constantly recurs to the subject in his writings. He describes the awful agony of the condemned man and insists on the cruelty of inflicting such torture. Then followed four years of penal servitude, spent in the company of common criminals in Siberia, where he began the “Dead House,” and some years of service in a disciplinary battalion.
danish.translation: Denne oplevelses voldsomme lidelse satte et varigt præg på Dostojevskijs sind. Selv om hans religiøse sindelag til sidst fik ham til at acceptere enhver lidelse med resignation og i sit eget tilfælde betragte den som en velsignelse, vender han hele tiden tilbage til emnet i sine skrifter. Han beskriver den dødsdømtes frygtelige kvaler og understreger grusomheden i at påføre et menneske en sådan tortur. Derefter fulgte fire års strafarbejde blandt almindelige forbrydere i Sibirien, hvor han begyndte på »Det døde hus«, og nogle års tjeneste i en disciplinærbataljon.

danish.source: He had shown signs of some obscure nervous disease before his arrest and this now developed into violent attacks of epilepsy, from which he suffered for the rest of his life. The fits occurred three or four times a year and were more frequent in periods of great strain. In 1859 he was allowed to return to Russia. He started a journal—“Vremya,” which was forbidden by the Censorship through a misunderstanding. In 1864 he lost his first wife and his brother Mihail. He was in terrible poverty, yet he took upon himself the payment of his brother’s debts. He started another journal—“The Epoch,” which within a few months was also prohibited. He was weighed down by debt, his brother’s family was dependent on him, he was forced to write at heart-breaking speed, and is said never to have corrected his work. The later years of his life were much softened by the tenderness and devotion of his second wife.
danish.translation: Før arrestationen havde han vist tegn på en uafklaret nervesygdom, som nu udviklede sig til voldsomme epileptiske anfald, der plagede ham resten af livet. Anfaldene kom tre eller fire gange om året og hyppigere i perioder med stor belastning. I 1859 fik han lov til at vende tilbage til Rusland. Han grundlagde tidsskriftet »Vremja«, som på grund af en misforståelse blev forbudt af censuren. I 1864 mistede han sin første kone og sin bror Mikhail. Han levede i frygtelig fattigdom, men påtog sig alligevel at betale brorens gæld. Han grundlagde endnu et tidsskrift, »Epoken«, som efter få måneder også blev forbudt. Gælden tyngede ham, brorens familie var afhængig af ham, og han måtte skrive i et hjerteskærende tempo; det siges, at han aldrig rettede sine tekster. Hans anden kones ømhed og hengivenhed gjorde hans sidste leveår langt mildere.

danish.source: In June 1880 he made his famous speech at the unveiling of the monument to Pushkin in Moscow and he was received with extraordinary demonstrations of love and honour.
danish.translation: I juni 1880 holdt han sin berømte tale ved afsløringen af Pusjkin-monumentet i Moskva og blev mødt med usædvanligt stærke udtryk for kærlighed og hyldest.

danish.source: A few months later Dostoevsky died. He was followed to the grave by a vast multitude of mourners, who “gave the hapless man the funeral of a king.” He is still probably the most widely read writer in Russia.
danish.translation: Få måneder senere døde Dostojevskij. En vældig skare af sørgende fulgte ham til graven og »gav den ulykkelige mand en konges begravelse«. Han er sandsynligvis stadig den mest læste forfatter i Rusland.

danish.source: In the words of a Russian critic, who seeks to explain the feeling inspired by Dostoevsky: “He was one of ourselves, a man of our blood and our bone, but one who has suffered and has seen so much more deeply than we have his insight impresses us as wisdom... that wisdom of the heart which we seek that we may learn from it how to live. All his other gifts came to him from nature, this he won for himself and through it he became great.”
danish.translation: En russisk kritiker, som forsøger at forklare de følelser, Dostojevskij vækker, skriver: »Han var en af os, et menneske af vores eget kød og blod, men et menneske, der har lidt og set så meget dybere end vi; hans indsigt virker på os som visdom ... den hjertets visdom, vi søger for at lære af den, hvordan vi skal leve. Alle sine andre evner fik han af naturen; denne vandt han selv, og gennem den blev han stor.«
